questions.q: Why does this lesson say logging and auditing have to be deliberately designed for an integration, unlike for a human user session?
options: Salesforce automatically emails an admin every time an integration runs
There's no human present to notice something looking wrong, so nothing about an API call forces anyone to look at it afterward unless monitoring is built in
Integrations cannot generate any log data at all by default
Logging only applies to UI sessions, never to API activity
questions.explain: A human session gets informal monitoring for free, because a person notices when something seems off. An unattended integration has no equivalent unless logging and review are deliberately designed in.

questions.q: What is the main practical difference between historical event log data and real-time event monitoring?
options: They capture entirely unrelated kinds of data with no overlap
Real-time monitoring has no retention limit, while historical logs expire immediately
Historical event logs only cover login activity, never API activity
Historical event log data becomes queryable only after a processing delay and is retained for a limited window, while real-time monitoring streams events as they happen
questions.explain: Historical event log data is the after-the-fact investigation tool, available after a delay with limited retention; real-time monitoring is the detect-close-to-when-it-happens tool, requiring an active subscription to a stream.

questions.q: What does Setup Audit Trail track, as distinct from event monitoring?
options: The exact SOQL queries an integration user has run
Real-time API call volume by object
Changes to the org's own configuration -- who modified a permission set, a connected app's policy, or a Named Credential's settings
Setup Audit Trail and event monitoring track exactly the same data
questions.explain: Setup Audit Trail answers 'who changed how this integration is configured to behave,' a different axis from event monitoring's focus on what the integration's identity actually did -- a thorough review needs both.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say you need a documented baseline before event data becomes useful for spotting a problem?
options: Without knowing what normal volume, timing, and scope look like for a specific integration, there's no way to distinguish ordinary activity from something abnormal in the raw event data
A baseline is only needed for real-time monitoring, never for historical log review
Salesforce automatically computes a baseline for every integration user
Baselines are a compliance formality with no practical use
questions.explain: Raw event data is only informative relative to a known normal pattern -- observing an integration's real activity for a representative period and documenting it is what makes later alerting thresholds or review criteria meaningful rather than arbitrary.

questions.q: A security team only ever queries historical event log data for its integrations, never subscribing to real-time events. What limitation does this lesson say that creates?
options: This approach violates a Salesforce platform requirement
Historical event log data cannot capture API activity at all, only UI activity
No limitation -- historical data alone is always sufficient
They will reliably learn what happened, but only well after the fact, missing the chance to detect and react to something unusual close to when it occurs
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames this as a design mistake: historical-only monitoring is good for retrospective investigation but inherently delayed, so unusual activity close to when it happens won't be caught without also watching a real-time stream.
